Where it began

Damien Martyn was born in Darwin on 21 October 1971 and moved with his family to Perth when he was three. He went to Girrawheen Senior High School and in 1990 won a place at the Australian Cricket Academy in Adelaide.

A season later he was in the Western Australia side, and in his first summer of first-class cricket he scored 822 runs at 51.37. By the 1994–95 season, aged 23, he was captaining the state, the youngest player ever given the job, and he led Australia A in a one-day tournament that same summer. A year later he handed the captaincy to Tom Moody so he could think about his batting.

The player

He made his Test debut against the West Indies at the Gabba in November 1992, scoring 36 and 15. The early years were stop-start, and from 1994 he spent six years out of the Test side. He came back in 2000, and in the 2001 Ashes he made his first Test hundred, 105 at Edgbaston, nine years after his debut. Wisden made him one of its Cricketers of the Year for that summer.

Before long he had settled in at number four. In 67 Tests between 1992 and 2006 he scored 4,406 runs at 46.38, with 13 hundreds, 23 fifties and a best of 165 against New Zealand at Wellington in 2005. His richest spell began in March 2004: two hundreds in a 3–0 win in Sri Lanka, then man of the series as Australia won a series in India for the first time in over three decades. Over those 12 months he made 1,608 runs at 61.84 with seven hundreds. He also won the World Cup in 1999 and 2003 and the Champions Trophy in 2006, finishing that last one unbeaten in the final.

What made him special

He had a classical method and elegant strokes on the off side, square of the wicket and through the covers. In the field he was just as easy on the eye, a fine cover fielder who could produce a run-out from nowhere. He could bowl a little medium pace and, once in a while in first-class cricket, keep wicket.

As a young man his strokes were sometimes a step ahead of his patience, and he had to wait a long time for a second chance. When it came, he did not waste it.

Away from the middle

In 2005 he collected the McGilvray Medal, the ABC's award for the Test cricketer of the year, and was named Test Player of the Year at the Allan Border Medal. He surprised everyone in December 2006 by announcing his retirement from all cricket in the middle of an Ashes series, though in 2010 he signed for the Rajasthan Royals in the IPL. Adam Gilchrist, his old team-mate, was also a close friend.

And finally

He took only two Test wickets, at 84.00 apiece. But his best bowling figures were 1 for 0, and there is not much anyone can do to improve on that.
